extracted.intended_audience: Wikipedia editors writing or editing mathematics articles
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for composing and formatting encyclopedic mathematics articles on English Wikipedia, including structure, prose style, notation, typesetting, and field-specific conventions. Aimed at making articles accessible to general readers while retaining technical precision for specialists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address reader's level of knowledge / Structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Start simple and then move towards more abstract and technical subjects later on; decide whether to assume familiarity with background subjects (e.g., arithmetic, algebra, geometry) and structure the article accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Probably the hardest part is addressing a reader's level of knowledge. When in doubt, start with accessible material and progressively introduce technicalities. Use common sense and community consensus; substantive edits should reflect consensus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead (article introduction) purpose and accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The lead should describe and define the subject, provide context, and summarize the article's most important points; it should be accessible to a general reader and avoid specialized terminology and symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulas should appear in the first paragraph only if necessary (they won't display in link previews unless raw HTML or <math>). Include the article title/alternate names in bold. When appropriate, include historical motivation, an informal introduction, and applications. If an informal introduction is given, mark it as informal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid formulas in lead preview / formula display in lead
rubrics_metrics.description: Formulas should appear in the first paragraph only if necessary, since they will not be displayed in the preview that pops up when hovering over a link.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For having formulae displayed when hovering, they must be written in raw HTML or in LaTeX inside <math> tags (LaTeX source is shown without tags in preview). Prefer words in lead where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define notation and use standard notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles should define the notation they use; use standard notation when possible and define any non-standard or uncommon notation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If extensive notation is required, introduce it as a bulleted list or in a separate 'Notation' section. Each article should explain terminology as if there are no conventions to minimize confusion across articles and readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide exact/formal definitions when topic is an object
rubrics_metrics.description: An article about a mathematical object should provide an exact definition of the object, perhaps in a 'Definition' section after motivation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the phrase 'formal definition' to flag actual definitions for readers unfamiliar with academic terminology. Identify the nature of the entity being defined and avoid conflating definition with derived equations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem statements must be precise
rubrics_metrics.description: When the topic is a theorem, the article should provide a precise statement of the theorem, either in the lead or in its own section for long theorems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present equivalent formulations when appropriate; separate long statements into their own sections (e.g., Poincaré–Birkhoff–Witt).

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative examples and non-examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide representative examples and applications to illustrate definitions and theorems; non-examples may be useful to show almost-but-not-quite cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples should be informative rather than instructional (WP:NOTTEXTBOOK). Short examples fit inline; longer or many computational examples may deserve their own section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pictures and diagrams when helpful
rubrics_metrics.description: A picture can bring home a point and can often precede the mathematical discussion of a concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow guidance in 'How to create graphs for Wikipedia articles' for creation and inclusion. Diagrams should use the same conventions as the text referring to them; prefer the better illustration even if its convention differs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulas: explain or replace by words where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Formulas tend to repel less mathematical readers; mathematics articles should take pains to explain (or even replace) them by words if possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer English words 'for all', 'exists', and 'in' rather than ∀, ∃, ∈. Highlight definitions with phrases like 'is defined by' to distinguish definitions from equations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concluding matters: generalizations, 'See also', references
rubrics_metrics.description: Include material on generalizations when appropriate, a 'See also' section linking related subjects, and a 'References' section with literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'References' to enable verification and further reading (see § Including literature and references). 'See also' should link to related subjects or pages offering further insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not begin sentences with symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: In the interest of clarity, sentences should not begin with a symbol (e.g., do not start sentences with G, H, Δ alone).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewrite sentences so that the symbol appears mid-sentence or after an introductory phrase. Example of bad vs good given in the guideline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid textbook-style rhetorical devices and opinionated phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid leading questions, 'It follows easily that', and opinionated rhetorical devices that compromise encyclopedic tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide reasons or hints why things hold rather than rhetorical exhortations; reorganize text to put crucial parts first. Downplay the author's 'we' where helpful for tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid contentless clichés (e.g., 'It is easily seen that')
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid phrases like 'It is easily seen that', 'Clearly', 'It should be noted that', which presume the reader shares the author's insight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead, hint why something must hold or provide a short explanation or reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid blackboard abbreviations and jargon
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using abbreviations such as 'wrt', 'wlog', 'iff', and symbols like ∀ and ∃ verbatim in prose because they are jargon and may confuse readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spell out quantifiers and abbreviations in full for accessibility and encyclopedic prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ambiguous use of 'any'
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using 'any' when verbalizing quantifiers since it is ambiguous; prefer 'every' or 'some' as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., write 'if every x satisfies F(x)=0' or 'if some x satisfies F(x)=0' rather than 'if any x satisfies...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plural consistency for 'formula'/'formulae'
rubrics_metrics.description: Plural of 'formula' is either 'formulae' or 'formulas'; both acceptable but an article should be internally consistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not change a consistent article's usage solely to conform to another preference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical conventions: state and respect article-specific conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Conventions (terminology/notation) exist to bring uniformity, but each article may establish its own conventions; explain them if the article departs from common practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changing an article's conventions should not be done lightly; prefer prevalence in reliable sources and discuss mass changes on talk pages or with relevant Wikiprojects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology field-specific defaults (natural numbers, rings, schemes, topology)
rubrics_metrics.description: The manual provides default assumptions for field-specific terms (e.g., natural numbers may include 0 or not; a ring is assumed associative and unital; an algebraic variety is assumed irreducible; a compact space is not assumed Hausdorff).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the sense appropriate to the field; if unclear and important, use alternative explicit phrasing; when deviating, state the adopted convention in the article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notational conventions: common symbol usage and disambiguation
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer and document standard notations (e.g., Z_n vs C_n for cyclic groups, D_n vs D_2n for dihedral groups depending on context); indicate which convention is used in the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where two conflicting common conventions exist, clarify which is in use and be consistent. Examples include semidirect product notation K ×_φ Q or K ⋊ Q, subset symbols ⊆ vs ⊂ usage, transpose notation X^T or X^{	op}, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof inclusion guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Since Wikipedia is an encyclopedia not a collection of mathematical texts, include proofs when they expose or illuminate the concept or idea; omit proofs that serve only to establish correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set proofs apart (e.g., separate section) so readers who want to skip them can. See Wikipedia:WikiProject Mathematics/Proofs for additional guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithms: language choice and implementations
rubrics_metrics.description: An article about an algorithm may include pseudocode or source code; choose a language that expresses the algorithm clearly and avoid multiple implementations unless encyclopedic interest exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Source code should use syntax highlighting; do not include multiple implementations of the same algorithm in different languages unless each has encyclopedic interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include inline citations and references (WP:VERIFY)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is essential for article content to have inline citations and a well-chosen list of references and pointers to the literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations support further reading, verify usage/definitions, and give historical context for important theorems. Follow Wikipedia:Cite sources for formatting and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typesetting mathematics: prefer LaTeX (<math>) for displayed formulae
rubrics_metrics.description: For formulae on their own line the preferred formatting is LaTeX markup using the <math> tag; section headings must use HTML only (LaTeX may cause uneven spacing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not change formatting (LaTeX vs HTML) boldly across many articles without discussion. LaTeX renders as PNG/MathML/HTML depending on user preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inline LaTeX drawbacks and display=inline
rubrics_metrics.description: Inline LaTeX formulae can have larger font size, affect download speed, and not align well; use <math display=inline> or text-style commands to reduce size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use display=inline to generate smaller summation symbols and better baseline alignment; for simple inline formulae consider HTML-formatted expressions instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using indentation (colons) to produce displayed formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Indenting a line with colons to display formulae produces invalid HTML; use <math display=block> instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convert indented formulae to proper <math> markup when editing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Line-wrapping and no-wrap templates for inline math
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct use of <math> tags may introduce undesirable line-wrapping points; use templates like {{nobr}} or {{tmath}} to prevent awkward wrapping and font discordance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wrap LaTeX markup in {{nobr|<math>...</math>}} or use {{tmath}} to control wrapping and presentation; take care with adjacent punctuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alt text for LaTeX-generated images
rubrics_metrics.description: Images generated from LaTeX markup have alt text (default is the LaTeX markup); override with an explicit alt attribute for small, easily explained formulas to aid visually impaired readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alt text should be plain text without newlines or HTML; for complicated formulas, the default LaTeX markup is usually preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Font templates: use {{math}} and {{mvar}} for consistent serif/italics
rubrics_metrics.description: HTML math expressions should use the {{math}} template so they display in a serif font; use {{mvar}} to ensure an italic serif typeface for variables in text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using {{mvar}} helps distinguish certain characters and aids screen readers and spell-checkers. Avoid using double apostrophes for math content, which yields sans-serif rendering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variables italicization and descriptive subscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Use italic text for variables, but never for numbers or symbols; descriptive subscripts should not be italicized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Within {{math}} templates, use double apostrophes or {{mvar}} to italicize variables. SI units are never italicized (e.g., x = 5 cm).

rubrics_metrics.name: Function and operator name formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Names for standard functions (sin, cos, etc.) are upright (Roman); single-letter functions (f) are italic; for nonstandard multi-letter operators use \operatorname to get correct spacing and upright font.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not write 2sinx (incorrect); use 2\sin x or 2\sin(x+1) with parentheses when needed. Use \operatorname{tr} for operator names to get spacing right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greek letters: italicize lowercase when they are variables/constants
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize lower-case Greek letters when they are variables or constants; do not italicize capital Greek letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow LaTeX/math typesetting conventions; use the Greek letters (U+03BC μ rather than U+00B5) per Unicode guidance; be consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common sets notation and blackboard bold usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Common sets of numbers (e.g., ℝ) are typically typeset in boldface or blackboard bold; either is acceptable but be consistent within an article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid Unicode blackboard bold characters due to inconsistent rendering; prefer LaTeX \mathbb or bold; be aware of rendering bugs (e.g., blackboard bold with numerals) and use alternatives when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superscripts and subscripts: use <sup> and <sub> tags
rubrics_metrics.description: Superscripts and subscripts should be wrapped in <sup> and <sub> tags with no other formatting info; do not use special characters like ² for powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For TeX-rendered math, <sup> may be converted to image; use TeX for complex exponents and keep simple HTML for plain text compatibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special symbols: favor <math> rendering and safe Unicode choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Almost all mathematical operator symbols have specific Unicode code points, but not all browsers render them correctly; to guarantee display, force rendering with <math> LaTeX markup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer U+2032 for prime, U+2217 for asterisk operator where appropriate, U+002F for solidus, U+003A for colon etc., and avoid using visually inconsistent Unicode alternatives when <math> is available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Less-than sign in source
rubrics_metrics.description: Use < when writing the less-than sign in wiki source to avoid confusion with HTML tags.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., use {{math|'x' < 3}} rather than raw '<' inside <math> where HTML parsing could be affected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplication sign usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard algebraic notation is qd for q times d in formulae; use × (×) or the dot operator (⋅) when explaining to general audiences or in examples; do not use the letter 'x' or ASCII asterisk '*' outside source code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For general-audience exposition use ×; for dot operator use \cdot or ⋅. Avoid using 'x' as multiplication and avoid '*' outside code.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minus sign: use the true minus character
rubrics_metrics.description: The correct encoding of the minus sign '−' is different from hyphen '-' or en-dash '–'; use the dedicated minus character or −.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Except in source code, the hyphen-minus should not be visible as the rendered minus sign; use the proper character for typographic correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Radical symbol: prefer \sqrt in <math>
rubrics_metrics.description: Use <math>\sqrt{...}</math> rather than HTML radical or radic templates for complex expressions because HTML radicals often misalign the overline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of MediaWiki bugs, { {radic}} or bare √ may be used in image captions until fixes; simple expressions may use √ without overline if unambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain symbols in formulae in prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Lists of symbol definitions should be written as prose to avoid excess vertical space; exceptions for very long definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each definition within prose should end with comma/semicolon and the last with a period. Use prose unless definitions are very long (in which case a list may be justified).

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation after formulae
rubrics_metrics.description: A sentence that ends with a formula must have the appropriate punctuation (period, comma, etc.) at the end of the formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using <math>...</math> include the punctuation inside the tags so it doesn't wrap to a new line; alternatively, wrap formula plus punctuation in {{nowrap}} or use {{tmath}} for simple inline cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-letter names and operator names upright
rubrics_metrics.description: Functions with multi-letter names should be in an upright (Roman) font; single-letter function names like f are italic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omit parentheses for standard functions when unambiguous (2\sin x), but use parentheses when the argument is more than a single term. Use \operatorname for custom multi-letter operators to get correct spacing and upright font.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subscript label font distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Subscripts that are variables or constants should be italic, while textual labels in subscripts should be upright (Roman).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use \text{...} inside math to make subscripts upright when they are words or labels (e.g., x_{predicted} is incorrect; x_{\text{predicted}} is correct).

rubrics_metrics.name: Roman vs italic choices: be article-consistent
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Roman or italic styles consistently within an article; do not perform mass changes to conform to one external style without discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When in dispute, prefer prevalence in reliable sources and discuss on talk pages; formatting changes should aim for internal consistency rather than global uniformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blackboard bold rendering caveats
rubrics_metrics.description: Use LaTeX rendering (\mathbb{R}) or bold rather than Unicode blackboard bold characters because Unicode support is inconsistent; be consistent within the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Due to rendering bugs, LaTeX blackboard bold may not work with numerals; use bold or Unicode only when necessary and justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fractions: prefer horizontal bar or slash; avoid {{frac}} and precomposed Unicode fractions
rubrics_metrics.description: In mathematics articles, fractions should be written with a horizontal fraction bar or with a forward slash; the {{frac}} template and Unicode precomposed fractions are discouraged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use \textstyle\frac{1}{2} or 1/2 depending on context. Metric units use decimals not fractions; non-metric units follow reliable-source practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphs and diagrams: consistent labeling conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no universal agreement on fonts for graphs and diagrams, but for geometry points are normally labelled with uppercase letters, sides with lower case, angles with lower-case Greek.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For ease of reference diagrams should use the same conventions as the surrounding text; prefer the better illustration even if it uses different conventions, but document differences if necessary.
